enonce_markdown: The values 5, 8 and 2 are pushed onto an empty stack in that order. A pop operation is then performed. Which value is returned?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A stack is a last-in first-out (LIFO) structure: pop removes and returns the item that was pushed most recently.

### Solution

The last value pushed was 2, so the pop returns **2**; the stack then holds 5 and 8 (8 on top). The value 5 would be returned by a queue (first in, first out), and the stack is not empty.

choix.texte: Nothing, because the stack is empty

enonce_markdown: Three print jobs A, B and C are added, in that order, to a printer queue. The printer then takes two jobs from the queue. Which job is now at the front of the queue?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A queue is a first-in first-out (FIFO) structure: items leave from the front in the order in which they arrived.

### Solution

The printer takes A and then B, the first two jobs to arrive. The job now at the front is **C**.

enonce_markdown: A circular queue is implemented in an array whose indices run from 0 to 5 (capacity 6). The item at the front is stored at index 4 and the queue currently holds 4 items. At which index will the **next** item be stored?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

In a circular queue the index wraps around to 0 after the last position, so the next free index is (front + number of items) MOD capacity.

### Solution

The 4 items occupy indices 4, 5, 0 and 1. The next free index is $(4 + 4) \bmod 6 = 8 \bmod 6 = 2$. Without the wrap-around the result would be 8, which does not exist; 0 and 3 come from miscounting the items.

enonce_markdown: The values 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 are inserted, in that order, into an initially empty binary search tree (smaller values go to the left, larger values to the right). What output does a **post-order** traversal (left subtree, right subtree, then the node) produce?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Build the tree by inserting the values one at a time, then apply the traversal rule recursively: post-order visits the left subtree, the right subtree and finally the root of each subtree.

### Solution

The tree has 50 as root, 30 and 70 as its children, and 20, 40, 60, 80 as leaves. Post-order gives **20, 40, 30, 60, 80, 70, 50**. The sequence 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80 is the in-order traversal (sorted values), and 50, 30, 20, 40, 70, 60, 80 is the pre-order traversal.

A clinic keeps a waiting list in which new patients are often added at the **front** of the list when they are emergencies, and patients are often removed from the middle when they leave without being seen. The list is read in order but rarely accessed by position.

(a) Explain why a linked list is more suitable than an array for this list. (4 marks)

(b) Give one disadvantage of a linked list compared with an array. (2 marks)
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Compare how each structure performs the operations that are frequent: an array stores items contiguously and must shift items to insert or delete; a linked list stores nodes with pointers, so insertion and deletion only change pointers.

### Solution

**(a)** In an array, inserting at the front or removing from the middle forces all the following items to be shifted, which is $O(n)$ for each operation. In a linked list, inserting at the front creates a node and changes the head pointer, which is $O(1)$; removing a node from the middle only needs the pointer of the previous node to be changed (once the node has been located). The list also grows and shrinks dynamically, with no fixed size to declare. Since the list is read in order and not by position, the fast direct access of an array is not needed.

**(b)** Any one of: no direct access by position (the nodes must be followed one by one, $O(n)$); each node needs extra memory for the pointer; more complex to program (risk of lost pointers).

enonce_markdown:
A postfix (reverse Polish) expression is evaluated with a stack: a number is pushed; an operator pops the top two items and pushes the result, where the **second item popped** is the left operand. The expression is:

`3 4 + 2 * 7 -`

What value is left on the stack at the end?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Scan the tokens from left to right. For an operator, pop the right operand first, then the left operand, apply the operator as left op right, and push the result.

### Solution

| Token | Stack after (top on the right) |
|---|---|
| 3 | 3 |
| 4 | 3 4 |
| + | 7 |
| 2 | 7 2 |
| * | 14 |
| 7 | 14 7 |
| - | 7 |

The last operation is $14 - 7 = 7$, so the stack holds **7** (the expression is $(3 + 4) \times 2 - 7$). The value -7 comes from swapping the operands of the subtraction, 14 comes from stopping before the last operator, and 4 is the result of ignoring the order given by the postfix form ($3 + 4 \times 2 - 7$).
